entries.question: Explain the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect. When would you use one over the other? Write a custom hook that debounces a value and explain why useEffect is appropriate there.
entries.expectedApproach: useEffect runs asynchronously after paint, useLayoutEffect runs synchronously before paint. Use useLayoutEffect for DOM measurements/mutations that must happen before user sees the update (e.g., tooltip positioning). Debounce hook: use useEffect with setTimeout, clean up with clearTimeout in the return function.
keyPoints: useEffect is non-blocking (deferred after paint)
useLayoutEffect blocks the browser paint (synchronous)
Cleanup function runs before next effect and on unmount
Custom hooks must follow Rules of Hooks
followUps: How would you implement an infinite scroll hook using useEffect?
What are the performance implications of useLayoutEffect?
How does React 18 concurrent mode affect useEffect behavior?

entries.question: You're building a large-scale React dashboard with deeply nested components that all need access to user preferences, theme, and real-time notification data. Compare Context API, Redux, and Zustand. What would you choose and why?
entries.expectedApproach: Context: simple but triggers full subtree re-renders on any change. Redux: predictable, great DevTools, boilerplate-heavy, good for complex state logic. Zustand: minimal API, selective subscriptions (no re-render issue), great for medium-to-large apps. For this case: Zustand for preferences/theme (simple, performant) + separate Context for auth, WebSocket for real-time notifications. Avoid putting rapidly-changing data in Context.
keyPoints: Context API re-renders all consumers on any state change
Redux is best when you need time-travel debugging and middleware
Zustand/Jotai offer surgical re-renders via selectors
Don't put everything in one global store — separate concerns
followUps: How would you handle server state (API data) vs client state?
Compare React Query/TanStack Query with Redux for API data
How would you implement optimistic updates?

entries.question: Explain the JavaScript event loop, microtask queue, and macrotask queue. Given this code, predict the output order: console.log('1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); console.log('4');
entries.expectedApproach: Output: 1, 4, 3, 2. Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Promise.then() goes to microtask queue (3). setTimeout goes to macrotask queue (2). Microtasks are processed before the next macrotask. Event loop: call stack → microtasks (all) → one macrotask → microtasks → repeat.
keyPoints: Call stack executes synchronous code first
Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) drain completely before macrotasks
Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering
Each macrotask is followed by draining all microtasks
followUps: What happens if a microtask enqueues another microtask?
How does requestAnimationFrame fit into the event loop?
Explain how async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises

entries.question: Implement a responsive grid layout that shows 4 columns on desktop, 2 on tablet, and 1 on mobile. Use CSS Grid. Also explain the difference between minmax(), auto-fill, and auto-fit.
entries.expectedApproach: Use CSS Grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)); for automatic responsiveness. Or use explicit breakpoints with @media queries. auto-fill creates as many tracks as possible (may leave empty tracks), auto-fit collapses empty tracks. minmax() sets minimum and maximum track sizes.
keyPoints: CSS Grid with auto-fit/minmax() enables responsive layouts without media queries
auto-fill: keeps empty tracks, auto-fit: collapses empty tracks to fill space
fr unit distributes remaining space proportionally
Mobile-first approach: start with 1 column, add columns at breakpoints
followUps: When would you use Flexbox vs Grid?
How would you implement a masonry layout with CSS Grid?
Explain the CSS container queries and how they differ from media queries

entries.question: A React application has a First Contentful Paint (FCP) of 4.5 seconds and a Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) of 7 seconds. Walk through your debugging and optimization process to bring these under the 'Good' thresholds.
entries.expectedApproach: Good thresholds: FCP < 1.8s, LCP < 2.5s. Debug: Use Chrome DevTools Performance tab, Lighthouse, Web Vitals extension. Common fixes: (1) Code splitting with React.lazy + Suspense, (2) Image optimization (WebP, lazy loading, srcset), (3) Critical CSS inlining, (4) Server-side rendering or static generation, (5) Reduce JS bundle (tree shaking, dynamic imports), (6) CDN for assets, (7) Preconnect/preload for critical resources.
keyPoints: LCP targets: < 2.5s good, < 4.0s needs improvement, > 4.0s poor
Code splitting is the #1 quick win for React apps
Image optimization often has the largest impact on LCP
Measure before and after every optimization
followUps: How does React 18 streaming SSR improve TTFB and FCP?
Explain Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) and how to fix it
How would you implement progressive hydration?

entries.question: Explain the browser's critical rendering path. What happens between receiving the HTML response and the first pixel appearing on screen?
entries.expectedApproach: 1. Parse HTML → build DOM tree. 2. Parse CSS → build CSSOM. 3. Combine DOM + CSSOM → Render Tree (visible elements only). 4. Layout (reflow): calculate exact position and size of each element. 5. Paint: fill in pixels (colors, borders, shadows, text). 6. Composite: layer management, GPU compositing. JS can block parsing unless async/defer. CSS blocks rendering.
keyPoints: HTML parsing can be blocked by synchronous <script> tags
CSS is render-blocking: browser won't paint until CSSOM is ready
async vs defer: async = download + execute ASAP; defer = download now, execute after parsing
Compositor layers enable GPU-accelerated animations (transform, opacity)
followUps: What's the difference between a repaint and a reflow?
Which CSS properties trigger layout vs paint vs composite?
How does virtual DOM diffing relate to the rendering pipeline?

entries.question: Write a TypeScript generic type 'DeepReadonly<T>' that makes all properties of an object and all nested objects recursively readonly. Then write a type 'PickByType<T, ValueType>' that picks only properties of a specific type.
entries.expectedApproach: DeepReadonly: use mapped type with conditional recursion: type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }. PickByType: use key filtering: type PickByType<T, V> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K] }.
keyPoints: Mapped types iterate over keys of an object type
Conditional types (extends) enable type-level if/else
Key remapping (as clause) can filter keys
Recursive types need a base case to avoid infinite recursion
followUps: How would you make DeepReadonly handle arrays and tuples?
Explain the difference between 'type' and 'interface' for this use case
Write a type that converts union to intersection

entries.question: You're building a custom dropdown/select component in React. How would you make it fully accessible? Cover keyboard navigation, screen reader support, and ARIA attributes.
entries.expectedApproach: Use role='listbox' for the dropdown, role='option' for items. aria-expanded on trigger button, aria-activedescendant for focused option, aria-selected for selected option. Keyboard: Enter/Space to open, Up/Down to navigate, Escape to close, Home/End for first/last. Focus management: focus trap when open, return focus to trigger on close.
keyPoints: WCAG 2.1 AA compliance is the standard target
Prefer native HTML elements (<select>, <button>) when possible
aria-live='polite' for dynamic content announcements
Test with actual screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver), not just ARIA validators
followUps: How do you handle focus management in a modal dialog?
What's the difference between aria-label, aria-labelledby, and aria-describedby?
How would you test accessibility in CI/CD?
